newsitem.title: UK: Science journal defends cloning research.
newsitem.headline: Science journal defends cloning research.

text.p: The British scientific journal Nature, which published controversial research describing the cloning of an adult sheep, on Wednesday defended the study and said the debate that ensued was long overdue.
Ian Wilmut and colleagues at Scotland's Roslin Institute caused an uproar when they said they had created the first successful clone from an adult animal cell.
Presidents, Nobel laureates and newspapers all expressed alarm, with U.S. President Bill Clinton ordering an urgent inquiry into the ethics of cloning.
France's farm minister Philippe Vasseur invoked visions of "six-legged chickens" and there was widespread speculation that the process might work just as well on humans.
Nobel peace prize winner Joseph Rotblat, comparing the breakthrough with the creation of the atom bomb, urged the creation of ethical committees that could stop such frightening projects.
Nature itself said it had received an e-mail from an unnamed academic at Harvard University begging it not to publish the paper.
"As the procedure becomes more and more commonplace, abuse by extralegal or foreign groups is almost inevitable," it quoted the academic as saying.
"The writer is correct to imply that discussion has been grossly inadequate," Nature, one of the world's most respected scientific journals, said in a commentary.

"At a time when the science policy world is replete with technology foresight exercises, for a U.S. president and other politicians only now to be requesting guidance about what appears in today's Nature is shaming."
Nature pointed out that the same group had cloned two sheep last year using embryonic cells and said the work with adult cells was inevitable.
Britons have been congratulating themselves on their extensive attention to the problem.

Wilmut's group reported on their work to both the government-appointed Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority (HFEA) and the Nuffield Council on Bioethics, a committee of scientists, doctors and other experts.
Both panels have discussed and reported on such issues at length.

For instance the Nuffield Council reported last year that using animal organs for human transplants would be ethically acceptable, as long as care was taken to make sure animal viruses did not infect humans and the animals were not mistreated.
